paper_title: S3AC: Stabilized, Selective, and Scalable Actor-Critic for LLM Reasoning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Critic-free methods are widely used in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, avoiding difficult and costly critic training. Common alternatives lack token-level credit assignment and typically rely on grouped rollouts to estimate prompt-specific baselines. A critic can address both limitations, but long-CoT critic training is hindered by insufficient coverage of trajectories with diverse lengths and early gradients dominated by the newly initialized value head. We introduce S3AC (Stabilized, Selective, and Scalable Actor-Critic) for LLM reasoning, built around a practical critic-training recipe. The trained critic provides token-specific advantages and prompt-specific baselines. Using the prompt-level baseline to estimate difficulty, we propose Difficulty-Aware Prompt Sampling (DAPS). DAPS combines this estimate with outcome history to select prompts before generation, reducing rollout waste without offline difficulty initialization. S3AC improves group-rollout performance across dense and mixture-of-experts models from 1.5B to 397B parameters, outperforming a modern GRPO variant (GRPO-X). At 35B, it sustains single-rollout training while tested critic-free baselines deteriorate after initial gains.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Critic-free methods are widely used in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, avoiding difficult and costly critic training. Common alternatives lack token-level credit assignment and typically rely on grouped rollouts to estimate prompt-specific baselines. critic can address both limitations, but longCoT critic training is hindered by insufficient coverage of trajectories with diverse lengths and early gradients dominated by the newly initialized value head. We introduce S3AC (Stabilized, Selective, and Scalable ActorCritic) for LLM reasoning, built around practical critictraining recipe. The trained critic provides token-specific advantages and prompt-specific baselines. Using the prompt-level baseline to estimate difficulty, we propose DifficultyAware Prompt Sampling (DAPS). DAPS combines this estimate with outcome history to select prompts before generation, reducing rollout waste without offline difficulty initialization. S3AC improves group-rollout performance across dense and mixture-of-experts models from 1.5B to 397B parameters, outperforming modern GRPO variant (GRPO-X). At 35B, it sustains single-rollout training while tested critic-free baselines deteriorate after initial gains.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Critic-free methods, including GRPO, are widely used in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for large language model (LLM) reasoning (DeepSeek-AI, 2026; Kimi Team, 2026a,b; LLM-Core Xiaomi, 2026; Intern-S2-Preview Team, 2026). They avoid the difficulty and cost of training value model for long responses under sparse rewards and an evolving policy. However, replacing the critic with reward statistics limits how learning signals distinguish prompts and reasoning steps. *Corresponding authors. 1 failure may be expected on difficult prompt but surprising on an easy one, motivating promptspecific baseline. GRPO estimates this baseline from grouped rollouts, requiring each group to wait for its slowest response (Xu and Ding, 2026; Hou et al., 2026). Common single-rollout alternatives, including REINFORCE++ (Hu et al., 2025) and FlashREINFORCE (Hu et al., 2026), use batch statistics instead. These shared baselines do not account for differences in prompt difficulty. Even with prompt-specific baseline, single response-level advantage cannot distinguish the contributions of individual tokens. When an answer is incorrect, useful intermediate reasoning can receive the same negative signal as steps that lead away from solution (Wu et al., 2026). This scalar signal does not reflect how the difficulty of reaching correct answer changes as reasoning progresses. learned critic offers common route to addressing both limitations: prompt-conditioned baseline without grouped rollouts and tokenspecific learning signals throughout the response (Sutton et al., 1999). However, learning reliable value estimates for long reasoning trajectories remains challenging. Our analysis highlights two obstacles to effective value learning: initial-policy trajectories provide limited supervision on long, correct responses, while early gradients can be dominated by the newly initialized value head. To address these obstacles, we introduce S3AC (Stabilized, Selective, and Scalable ActorCritic) for LLM reasoning (Figure 1). We pretrain the critic on trajectories from policies of different strengths to broaden coverage across response lengths and outcomes. Small-scale value-head initialization controls initial predictions, while larger gradient-clipping threshold reduces excessive rescaling of backbone updates by headdominated gradients. Updated online, the critic provides difficulty-aware, token-specific advantages Figure 1: Overview of S3AC for long-CoT RLVR. (a) Critic value pretraining and online updates (3.3). (b) DAPS selects prompts using critic values and outcome history (3.4). (c) S3AC uses token-level GAE advantages; critic-free methods share one advantage across the response (3.2). throughout the response through generalized advantage estimation (Schulman et al., 2016). The critics usefulness extends to deciding what to generate. Because its prompt-conditioned estimate is available before rollout, it can guide prompt selection as well as policy learning. We propose Difficulty-Aware Prompt Sampling (DAPS), which combines this estimate with outcome history to select prompts of intermediate estimated difficulty. Some existing selectors require offline-initialized statistics or an auxiliary value model (Xu and Ding, 2026; Gao et al., 2026); DAPS reuses the critic already trained for policy learning. We evaluate two dense and two multimodal mixture-of-experts models spanning 1.5B to 397B parameters. Under group rollout, actorcritic training improves average performance across all four models, outperforming GRPO-X on all seven evaluated benchmarks at 35B and all five at 397B. At 35B, it sustains single-rollout performance while the tested critic-free baselines decline after initial gains (Figure 4). DAPS further improves both rollout settings over uniform prompt sampling and reduces trajectories discarded by group filtering.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Carlo rollouts, explained-variance gating, and critic ensembles, respectively. SAO (Hou et al., 2026) and CompactionRL (Li et al., 2026) apply PPO to single-rollout training of large MoE models. While these methods address different aspects of actor critic training, our work brings critic initialization, online value learning, and critic-guided prompt selection together in unified framework. Our study combines targeted diagnostics and ablations with evaluations across rollout settings and model scales, including group-rollout training at 397B parameters. Critic-free RL. Group-based methods such as GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), RLOO (Ahmadian et al., 2024), and DAPO (Yu et al., 2025) derive baselines from multiple responses to the same prompt. Single-rollout methods use batch statistics (REINFORCE++; Hu et al., 2025), add sequence-level trust region to batch-mean baseline (FlashREINFORCE; Hu et al., 2026), or track per-prompt values with tabular estimator (SPO; Xu and Ding, 2026). These methods typically construct advantages from sequence-level reward statistics without learning value function over intermediate response prefixes. Critic-based RL. PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) uses learned critic with GAE (Schulman et al., 2016) to estimate advantages for policy optimization. For long-CoT reasoning, VC-PPO (Yuan et al., 2025) pretrains the value model and decouples the GAE parameters of the actor and critic, while VAPO (Yue et al., 2025b) adapts λ to response length. VinePPO (Kazemnejad et al., 2025), EVPO (Pan et al., 2026), and AsyPPO (Liu et al., 2026) improve value estimates through Monte Difficulty-aware prompt sampling. Dynamic sampling (Yu et al., 2025) requires multiple responses per prompt and discards responses from uninformative groups after generation. Other methods estimate difficulty before rollout from reward history (GRESO; Zheng et al., 2025), from tracker initialized with offline rollouts (SPO), or from separately trained prompt-level value model (PCL; Gao et al., 2026). DAPS combines pass-rate history with value estimates from the existing S3AC critic, 2 avoiding separately trained difficulty model and supporting both group and single rollout.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: S3AC is an actorcritic framework for long-CoT RLVR that trains value model for both policy learning and prompt selection (Figure 1). The critic provides prompt-conditioned baselines and tokenspecific advantages, while its initial-state value guides prompt sampling before generation. We first formulate the actorcritic update (3.1), then examine the critics role under group and single rollout (3.2), describe its training recipe (3.3), and introduce DAPS (3.4).

sections.title: 3.2 How the Critic Shapes Learning Signals
sections.content: We examine how the critic shapes learning signals across prompts of different difficulty and across positions within response. The initial critic value Vϕ(s0) estimates the policys expected return for prompt before generation. Figure 2a plots these values against mean Monte Carlo (MC) returns from independent rollouts, using frozen 35B actor critic pair with one point per prompt. The values track differences in empirical returns, supporting their use as prompt-specific baselines. The promptspecific baseline is not limited to the initial position: subsequent values remain conditioned on the prompt throughout the response. Figure 2b illustrates this distinction in long failed responses: although all receive the same terminal reward of 1, their mean raw advantages remain close to zero for hard prompts and below 1 for easy prompts across response progress. Within response, expected returns can also change as reasoning progresses. shared response3 phasizes larger pretraining corpora. However, data scale alone does not ensure coverage of long, correct responses. We pool trajectories from policies of different strengths to broaden coverage across response lengths and outcomes, improving early online value prediction and downstream learning progress in our comparison (4.3). We pretrain for two epochs with token-averaged MSE against terminal returns, freezing attention layers following SAO (Hou et al., 2026) and additionally freezing the MoE router. Value-head optimization. In our runs, critic training exhibits much larger gradient norms than actor training, with the newly initialized value head dominating early pretraining gradients (4.3). For linear value head vt = wht, residual et = vt R, and loss ℓt = 1 2 e2 , wℓt = etht, htℓt = etw. The head gradient depends directly on hidden states, whereas the gradient entering the backbone is scaled by the small head weights. Global clipping driven by the head therefore also shrinks the much smaller backbone gradients. We initialize the head with standard deviation 1/(H+1), where is the hidden size, to control initial predictions. We also raise the gradient-clipping threshold from 1, common actor-training setting, to 10 for the critic, reducing excessive rescaling of backbone updates. Online adaptation. We update the critic on fresh rollouts as the policy evolves. Motivated by twotimescale actorcritic learning (Konda and Tsitsiklis, 1999), we use critic learning rate five times the actors and two critic epochs per rollout batch versus one actor epoch. We decouple actor and critic GAE following VC-PPO (Yuan et al., 2025). The critic regresses on Monte Carlo returns (λcritic = 1), while the actor uses VAPOs length-adaptive GAE (Yue et al., 2025b), λactor = 1 1 αT , where is the response length and α = 1.5.

sections.title: 3.4 Difficulty-Aware Prompt Sampling
sections.content: The same critic can also help decide which prompts the actor should attempt. In our group-rollout experiments, DAPO-style dynamic sampling (Yu et al., 2025) improves S3AC over retaining all groups, but it discards groups only after their responses have been generated. We therefore propose Figure 3: Critic values on Intern-S2-Preview-35B rise as the response identifies candidate values (A) and determines the requested term, 4/5 (B). Expanded examples are in Appendix C.2. level advantage cannot reflect these changes. Figure 3 illustrates this behavior with pretrained critic: its value rises when the response identifies candidate values and increases further when it determines the requested term. GAE combines these evolving values with the observed reward to construct token-specific advantages, allowing different positions within response to receive different learning signals. Under group rollout, the group mean already provides prompt-specific baseline, while the critic adds token-level advantages. Under single rollout, it also supplies the prompt-specific baseline missing from batch statistics. Our experiments show that S3AC outperforms GRPO-X under group rollout and sustains stable single-rollout training at 35B. These benefits require informative values across prompts and response positions, motivating the critic-training recipe in 3.3.

sections.title: 3.3 Training a Good Critic
sections.content: We initialize the critic through value pretraining and then update it online as the policy evolves. Our pretraining recipe addresses two challenges: limited coverage of long, correct trajectories and optimization dominated by the newly initialized value head. Coverage-oriented value pretraining. VC-PPO (Yuan et al., 2025) uses trajectories from fixed initial policy, while SAO (Hou et al., 2026) em4 Difficulty-Aware Prompt Sampling (DAPS), which combines the initial critic value with outcome history to guide prompt selection before generation. sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Training details. We train two dense models, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B (Yang et al., 2024) and R1Distill-1.5B (Guo et al., 2025), and two MoE models, Intern-S2-Preview-35B (Intern-S2-Preview Team, 2026) and Intern-S2-397B (InternLM, 2026). 5 Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B is trained on the 7.5k DAPOMath subset used by FlashREINFORCE (Yu et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026), R1-Distill-1.5B on MATH1,460 (Qi et al., 2025), and the MoE models on inhouse prompt sets covering mathematics, instruction following, reasoning, physics, and chemistry. Group rollout uses K=16 responses per prompt for dense models and K=8 for MoE models; single rollout uses K=1. Each rollout batch is split into eight mini-batches and used for one actor epoch, yielding eight actor gradient steps. We report RL training progress in actor gradient steps throughout. We use asymmetric importance-weight clipping (clip-higher) and dynamic sampling under group rollout (Yu et al., 2025). To address traininginference mismatch (Yao et al., 2025), S3AC and GRPO-X combine token-level importance sampling with IcePoP masks (Team et al., 2025) and MIS-style sequence-level masking (Liu et al., 2025). We mask an entire response when its maximum token-level log-probability ratio between the training and rollout policies exceeds threshold. S3AC uses DAPS on Qwen2.5-Math1.5B, R1-Distill-1.5B, and Intern-S2-Preview-35B, and uniform sampling on Intern-S2-397B. Full training configurations appear in Appendix  (Table 6)  . Baselines. For group rollout, we use GRPO-X, modern variant of GRPO (Shao et al., 2024). For single rollout, we compare with REINFORCE++ (Hu et al., 2025) and FlashREINFORCE (Hu et al., 2026). sections.title: 4.2 Main Results
sections.content: We evaluate the complete S3AC recipe under group and single rollout with benchmark performance and training stability. Group rollout: gains beyond group baseline. Even when grouped responses already provide prompt-specific baseline, S3AC improves over GRPO-X (4.1; Tables 13). At 35B, the bestcheckpoint average increases from 76.4 to 80.5, with gains on all seven benchmarks. These gains extend to 397B, where S3AC raises the average from 85.1 to 87.3 and leads on all five benchmarks. Together with gains on both 1.5B models, this supports S3ACs scalability from 1.5B dense models to 397B MoE models. The gains are consistent with 3.2: beyond the prompt-level information captured by group rewards, the critic conditions on the evolving response prefix and provides different learning signals across token positions. Single rollout: performance gains and training stability. With one response per prompt, S3AC achieves scores comparable to its group-rollout results (Tables 2 and 3). On Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B and 35B, its advantage over the best critic-free baseline within each setting is larger under single rollout. At 35B, S3AC reaches 80.9 versus 70.4 for REINFORCE++, 10.5-point gain. This pattern is consistent with the critic supplying the prompt-specific baseline missing from batch-level reward statistics, alongside token-specific advantages (3.2). Figure 2 illustrates this distinction: despite identical terminal rewards, long failed responses receive mean advantages closer to zero for hard prompts and more negative for easy prompts. The full 35B training curves show sustained single-rollout learning (Figure 4a). Both critic-free baselines improve initially but then decline, while S3AC retains most of its gains through 1,600 gradient steps. REINFORCE++ exhibits rapid growth 6 Figure 4: Training dynamics on Intern-S2-Preview-35B: (a) seven-benchmark average, (b) rollout entropy, and (c) response length. S3AC uses DAPS. Figure 5: Coverage pretraining improves value prediction and learning progress on Intern-S2-Preview-35B, reaching higher final performance within the same actor-update budget (group rollout). in rollout entropy and response length, whereas FlashREINFORCE shifts toward shorter responses as its score declines (Figure 4b,c). These dynamics support S3ACs stabilized actorcritic design for sustained single-rollout training at 35B. Appendix provides full 35B benchmark curves, Qwen single-rollout dynamics, and training and evaluation statistics (Figures 89; Table 7). Stable 35B single-rollout training also extends to alternative policy losses  (Table 8)  . We next examine the pretraining choices in 3.3.

sections.title: 4.3 Analysis of Critic Pretraining
sections.content: We examine the proposed value-pretraining method of 3.3 on Intern-S2-Preview-35B; full setups and diagnostics are in Appendix C. Pretraining data: broader coverage improves value prediction and learning progress. Pretraining on trajectories from multiple policies yields more accurate critic early in online training. The motivation is limited coverage: among responses longer than 24K tokens, only 5.0% are correct in initial-policy samples, compared with 61.8% for the policy at gradient step 1,600 (Figure 10a,b). We compare coverage critic, pretrained on trajectories from policies of different strengths, with an on-policy critic, pretrained only on initial-policy trajectories. Both runs share the actor initialization and the online recipe under group rollout; the two recipes also differ in data amount (Appendix C.1). The coverage critic attains higher EV and lower value loss early in online training, and the gap narrows as the on-policy critic adapts online (Figure 5). In this comparison, coverage pretraining enables faster learning progress and higher final performance within the same actorupdate budget. Pretraining optimization: initialization and clipping. Consistent with the analysis in 3.3, the value head accounts for over 99% of the squared gradient norm during the first 10 critic updates on Intern-S2-Preview-35B, despite having only 2,048 parameters (Appendix C.3). We evaluate the initialization and clipping choices in Table 4. An initialization standard deviation of 0.01 is already below the standard Xavier scale for this head. sections.title: 4.4 Difficulty-Aware Prompt Sampling
sections.content: We now evaluate DAPS (3.4), the selective component of S3AC, which reuses the critic for prompt selection before generation. We compare DAPS with uniform sampling using matched actor and critic initialization and the same S3AC training recipe within each pair. Detailed training and sampling settings are provided in Appendix D. Does critic-guided prompt selection improve learning? Within matched gradient-step budgets, DAPS improves the best evaluated S3AC score on both Intern-S2-Preview-35B and R1-Distill-1.5B under group and single rollout  (Table 5)  . Full training curves are provided in Appendix D. 8 Figure 6: DAPS sampling on Intern-S2-Preview-35B. (a) Trajectories discarded per rollout batch by the group filter. (b) Single-rollout training share on prompts with 0.2 < pref 0.8. Does selection before generation reduce waste? Under group rollout, DAPS reduces the number of trajectories discarded by dynamic sampling, with larger gap later in training (Figure 6a). Both methods retain the same number of trajectories per training batch, so fewer generated responses are lost to filtering. This supports the motivation in 3.4: selecting prompts before generation complements DAPO-style dynamic sampling by reducing generation spent on groups later discarded. Does DAPS help without group filter? The gains under single rollout show that DAPS also benefits training without group filtering. To examine which prompts enter training, we use each prompts success rate in completed uniform-sampling run, denoted by pref . After the initial sampling ramp, DAPS consistently allocates larger share of training trajectories to prompts with 0.2 < pref 0.8 (Figure 6b). This pattern is consistent with the acceptance rules preference for prompts of intermediate estimated difficulty (3.4).

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: S3AC enables effective critic training for longCoT RLVR through broader trajectory coverage, small-scale value-head initialization, and relaxed critic gradient clipping. The trained critic provides prompt-specific baselines and token-level advantages. Experiments show that this actorcritic approach outperforms GRPO-X under group rollout across 1.5B397B models and sustains stable single-rollout training at 35B. Beyond policy learning, DAPS reuses critic values and outcome history to select prompts before generation, reducing discarded responses under group rollout and improving performance in both settings.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Task scope. All experiments are reasoning-style tasks with verifiable rewards, namely math, science and multimodal reasoning. We do not evaluate agentic multi-turn settings, where credit must be assigned across tool calls and environment turns, so whether our findings carry over to agentic RL remains open. The reported experiments do not systematically assess variability across independent RL training seeds. Compute overhead. S3AC costs 2740% more amortized wall time per actor gradient step than GRPO-X, because the critic must be trained and run for inference alongside the policy.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: Our work aims to improve long-CoT reasoning in LLMs through RLVR. Higher benchmark scores do not establish the safety or reliability of model outputs in real-world applications; models may still generate incorrect or harmful content. Deployment requires application-specific evaluation and safeguards. Large-scale actorcritic training also requires additional computational resources and energy, and these costs should be weighed against the observed performance gains.

sections.title: A Experimental Details
sections.content: A.1 Training Configurations Our training pipeline is built on XTuner (XTuner Contributors, 2023), with LMDeploy (LMDeploy Contributors, 2023) used for rollout generation. Table 6 summarizes the training configurations; all methods start from the same base checkpoint within each model. All group-rollout runs use dynamic sampling (Yu et al., 2025), discarding groups whose responses are all correct or all incorrect. On Intern-S2-397B, both S3AC and GRPO-X apply an adaptive length regularizer that favors shorter correct responses in high-accuracy groups; S3AC uses the adjusted rewards for both actor and critic training. A.2 Evaluation We evaluate both 1.5B models offline at gradient step 1,024. For Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, we use temperature 0.7, top-p 0.7, and avg@16 on every benchmark. We cap the combined prompt and response length at 4,096 tokens; FlashREINFORCE (Hu et al., 2026) reports 4,096-token response budget. For R1-Distill-1.5B, we use temperature 0.8, top-p 0.95, 16,384-token response limit, and avg@32. Small score differences on R1-Distill-1.5B should be interpreted cautiously given the variability across repeated evaluations. For Intern-S2-Preview-35B and Intern-S2-397B, we use temperature 0.8 and top-p 1.0, with response limits of 64K and 62K tokens, respectively. We report avg@16 on AIME and HMMT26, avg@4 on GPQA-Diamond and IMO-AnswerBench, and avg@1 on the remaining benchmarks. A.3 Baselines GRPO-X uses the group z-score as the advantage, and REINFORCE++ normalizes the reward by the batch mean and standard deviation. The MoE GRPO-X baselines additionally use GEPO entropy control (Cheng et al., 2026), as described in 4.1. FlashREINFORCE follows its original configuration, with batch-mean baseline and sequencelevel trust region. sections.title: C Additional Critic Experiments
sections.content: This section provides token-level value examples for 3.2 and the experimental setups and diagnostics for 4.3. C.1 Experimental Setup Pretraining data and sources. For Intern-S2Preview-35B, the coverage critic learns from trajectories generated by policies of different strengths across multiple stages of prior experiments. Its preparation includes value pretraining on corpus of 327,680 trajectories (7.08B response tokens). The on-policy critic is pretrained only on 65,536 initial-policy trajectories (0.74B response tokens). At 1,600 actor gradient steps, the coverage and onpolicy runs achieve seven-benchmark averages of 80.78 and 79.86. Value-pretraining configuration. We pretrain for two epochs with cosine learning-rate decay from 105 to 5 106 after 3% linear warmup. The loss is 1 2 (Vϕ(st)R)2, averaged over response tokens using the terminal verifier reward R. The FP32 value head has initialization standard deviation 1/(H+1), and the gradient norm is clipped at 10. Attention, the MoE router and any vision tower and projector are frozen. Online configurations are given in 3.3 and Table 6. C.2 Data Coverage and Token-Level Values Response length and correctness. Figure 10 compares sampled trajectories from the initial policy and the policy at gradient step 1,600. Among responses longer than 24K tokens, 5.0% are correct in the initial-policy sample versus 61.8% at gradient step 1,600. The stronger-policy data thus supply long correct trajectories that are rare in the initial-policy data. Token-level value examples. Figure 11 expands the example in Figure 3 and adds numerical multiple-choice example, both evaluated with the coverage critic. In the first, the value rises when the response identifies the possible sequence values, including 4/5, and increases further when it determines that the requested term is 4/5. In the second, the value rises sharply from negative values toward zero after the response computes 0.1622 and matches it to option (0.1614). These examples illustrate how the coverage critic tracks meaningful reasoning progress within response, providing 15 Figure 10: Response-length distribution (a) and accuracy by length (b) for the initial policy and the policy at gradient step 1,600 on Intern-S2-Preview-35B. Bins span 2K tokens. fine-grained value estimates for token-level credit assignment. C.3 Value-Pretraining Optimization Gradient imbalance. Figure 12 reports the head and backbone gradient norms during the first 10 critic gradient steps of 35B value pretraining, supporting the analysis in 4.3. Figure 12: Head and backbone gradient norms over the first 10 critic gradient steps of 35B value pretraining, measured after distributed gradient reduction and before clipping. The dotted line marks the clipping threshold of 10. Figure 11: Illustrative critic values on Intern-S2-Preview-35B: (a) identifying candidate values (A) and determining the requested term, 4/5 (B); (b) matching 0.1622 to option (0.1614), with 150-token detail. Shaded ranges match the excerpts. Curves and colors show raw values before each response token; dashed lines mark reward +1. C.4 Value Pretraining at Different Model

sections.title: Scales
sections.content: We compare value pretraining at 35B and 397B. The 35B critic is pretrained on 1.13M trajectories (6.24B response tokens), and the Intern-S2397B critic on 1.85M trajectories (10.0B response tokens), using the configuration described in Appendix C.1. The 397B critic achieves lower and more stable value loss, together with smaller gradient norms (Figure 13), suggesting stronger value-fitting capacity for the larger critic in these runs. Figure 13: Value pretraining at 35B and 397B: (a) training value loss and (b) pre-clip gradient norm.
